Jane.—" Jack" would at fret sight appear to bee familiar abbreviation of John, and to be applied in that sense. It occurs in jaekdar, roaeting-jack, book-jack, jack-of-all- trades, jack-boots, jacloay (gin); jack, port of a machinery of a look mid of a pianoforte ; jack, an engine for raising heavy weights ; jack-knife, jack-towel, black.jock. In instances where the word occurs each as jack-am, jackdaw, jack-an-apes, jackm-lent, jack-pudding, it is manifestly derived front Jack, the familiar some for John ; but in the examples above cited the true etymology is to be found in the Celtic or Gaelic deagh (d before the vowel. e and i is pronounced j). Dmgh (or jeagh), the Cymric da signifies good, fit, appropriate, excellent, well. A jack-tor lea good sailor ; a roasting-jack is an instrument fit, appropriate, or good for the purpose of roasting. k jaCk-Of.all-trades is one et to turn his hand to anything useful ; a jack-knife is a good, useful, ancl large hour; a bootjack is good to pull off boots. Jackey, a slang word for English gin, means also strong ale, and among children a specks of eweetmeat, and is in all them cams synonymous with something good, as the French rail sweetrnmt a bon-bon, or as the Scotch call them goodies. Black-jack Is an old name for a large bottle of black leather, good to bold leer and other liquors. I find in a'Newcastle paper the following contribution front • correspondent on the very question " E. H." puts under the beading Notes, questions, and answers," in not sveelt Examiner, and I think it will fully answer his query :—Headera of Mrs. Henry Wood's popular novel, East Lynne," will remember Hat the authoress introduces I the story of a corpse being detained for debt. I have col- lected some curious notes on this subject. In the church- ! yard of North Wingfield, Derbyshire, a gravestone hears the liollowing inscription: "In memory of Thomas, son of John and Mary Clay, who departed this life December 181.11, 1724, in the 40th year of his age. - • • • • - •

la'hat theughZ mournful kindred stand Angund the solemn bier, Wo parents wrtng the twmbllng hand. Or drop the silent tear ; No ocatly osk adorned with art Pay weary limbs Inclese ; No friends impart • winding sheet To deck n.y last renew." The mime of the foregoing epitaph is thus explained: Thos. Clay waa 00.00 of intemperate habit, and at the time of his death was indebted to the village innkeeper, named Adlington. to the amount of no. The publican resolved to !adze the body; but the parents of the deceased carefully kept the door locked until the day appointed forthe funeral. As soon as the door was opened Adlington rushed into the bonne, seized the corpse, and placed it on • form in the open street, in front of the residence of the pirents of the de- parted. Clay's friends refueed to pay the publican'. account. After the body had been exposed for several days. Adlingten Committed it to the ground in a bacon chi*. I find in the Gentleman's Moyarint for November, Ism the following record of • corpee being seized in Lon'. Vl'esinesday, October 113th, I9ll.—As a funeral procession was preparing to proceed from lloston to Shoreslitch burial ground, the ceremony wa, prevented by a sheriff's officer and his aasis- tants, who, having presented a writ, removed the toaly into a shell, and con,eyed it assay. The authors°, this disgrace- ful proceeding applied the following day to the minion.. of Shoreditch to inter the corpee, which be very properly fused, unless the service swam read over it, which would in- sure the security of the body in holy ground. Ihe sheriffs have caused inquiry tube instituted into the circurnstancre or the cme; and finding that, though the racer did not dis- turb the body birnaelf, he improperly left it with the plain- tiff without having made any communication at the Sheriff's 1/flice, they have dismiteed him from hie emplov- ment." Another instance of the strange custom of wising and detaining a body fur debt occurs in the parish register of Sparsholt, Berkshire :—" Memorandum.—The corp. of John Matthews, of Fowler, was atopt on the Churchway for deld. Aug. 27th, 1680. And having laine there tower days, was hy Justices' warrant buried in the place to prevent annoyance.. hut about rise weeks after it wae boon Order Of Sessions taken up and buryed in the Churchyard by the wife of the deceased." The following extracts from Baines s Directory and thiseteer, published in 1825 (before the eatablisliment of railways), may not only be an answer to the question asked by "J. Sims,' but may prove interesting to others to observe what use their grandfathers made of the cansl for getting from place to place :—On the Marquis of Stafford's Canal (late Duke of Bridgewater's) goods were conveyed daily from Castle ,Ittay, Knott Mill, Manchester, to Worsley, Runcorn, Liverpool, and the iaterinediato plices. The beats used to start at 8 o'clock in the morning, cud arrival at Lon- don Bridge, Warrington, at noon, where coaches were in readiness to convey the passengers to Warrington and Liver- pool. At half-past three the same day the boat arrived at Runcorn, where a transference of passengers and luggage took place to a steam packet en route to Liverpool. I )aily " runs" were made from Runcorn to Manchester in eight hours. Extra steam and passage boats were tined during the summer months, their periods of departure being regu. lated by the fides. A passage boat left London Bridge, Warrington, every Satunlay morning, at 5 o'clock, arriving at Lyrom alit o'clock, Altrincham at 8, and Manchester at 10, returning the same day at 4 o'clock. A boat also con- veyed paseengern and luggage to Liverpool and Southport by Barton, Wormley, Astley, and Leigh. This boat arrived at Warrington at 1: o'clock at noon, and Liverpool at fl o'clock at night. In answer to "J. D.," let me nay that the original Cal- vinist Baptist no in Liverpool was a branch of a rociety at llill Cliff.. near Warrington, and went to Liver- ! pool about the year 1700. In 1714 they built a chapel in Liverpool, in Everton-lane, where a burial ground, I believe, yet remains. From this place the congregation, about the year 1799, removed to a new building to Byrom-street. and in 1789 to a larger building in the same etreet. Many other connected with the same body have since been erected in Liverpool. J. Si., Warrington.

This county first sent members in the 22nd of Edward 1., and has con- tinued the practice without intermission to the pressnt time. Originally two representatives were summoned from Lan- caster in the room of two ancient barons; two from Clitheroe, Instead of Baron Clitherosi and Baron Nether- wyrenclale; two from Preston, to represent the Barons of Penwortham and Wee°, two from Wigan, to represent m i interests not specified; two fro Newton, n lieu of the ancient Barons of Warrington and Belford ; and two from Liverpool for the Barony of Wydnen, and of Derby Hundred ; making twelve burgeeses to represent the ancient herons by tenure, in addit ion to the two knights, to represent the corn- moodily of the county." Mr. FAIIRINOTON reported as follows:—Having received an intimation of the existence of a nuisance st the Rig Fool, eitu ate in the townships of R,Hcoru and Halton, caused by the dr drug. of four proprietors situate in Halton, within your district, emptying into the said pool. I proceeded to in- spect the place on the Bth [net , and I have now to report that I found the quantity of sewage which emanates from the four properties to be very small indeed, and not of such a nature 13 10 cause the nuisance con plains,' of. I must certainly grant that a quantity of vegetable refuse had been removed previous to my visit, by directions given by the Runcorn surveyor, and the nuisance might be somewhat lessened. In making a minute inspection of the said pool, I eras somewhat surprised to find a large quantity of sewage flowing into it. Upon tracing the source of this, I was led to believe that it emanated from somewhere about 80 houses situate in Union and Sewedstreets, within the district of the Runcorn Improvement Commissioners. In its coarse to the pool this large volume of sewage passes through an an- trapped road inlet or covgaml, and Ille smell which proceeds from iris highly offensive. Hausa., Monday.—l mace Bismarck a Customs pollcy encounters great hostilities here. The Imperial Chancellor, in his new capacity as Minister of Commerce, is aiming at tile realisation of an economic dream, the first consequence of which would be Us inflict upon France a kind of customs ostracism uPon the Continent. Germany and Austria, ac- cording to Ids plan, would give notice of withdrawal from the treaties of commerce, and revert to the system of general tariffs: the most favoured nation clause would disappear, the two Empires would make each other considerable con- cessions, and would then endeavour to make Russia and Italy enter their customs union. Viscount Sandon, M.P., In responding foe the House of Commons, expressett his opinion that the House and the country were entilering from erestalk. With regent to the measures of the late session, he assured his hearers that il they proved to be for the benefit of the country no one would rejoice store than the members of the late Government, who, though attacked in a somewhat bitter

spirit, were theinselves determined to give their onpotients credit for honesty of purpotie. If the measures inlinded for the benefit of the farmers turned nut to be something more than mere good wishes—though he /CAA inclined to think they were not very subst aMial —he was sure they would all rejoice, for anything which benefitted the great agricultural interest must benefit the whole nation. Tat SPl,l[l,ll on Faunneu.—At Glynde Harvest Home, I on Saturday. the Speaker of the House of Commons gave his annual address to those engaged on his estate. lie said he hid been a farmer 30 years, and threaghout that period had keenly watched the harvest periods from year to year. The weather during the late harvest bad been among the hest ever enjoyed,. fart, bit knowledge wont Ile thought be could speak with confidence in stating lb rt the harvest period of last year was one of the wenn on record. He had prepared • statement abowirg the rainfall. mushine, and number of rainy days during the months of January to September, 1879.80. The facts were very interesting. They ebowed thet in August of last year the fall of rain was nearly ein Inches. while during the corresranding period this year the depth was less than an inch. The average rainfall of the Idistrict was rather over two inches per month, and, there- fore, the disastroue consequences attending the gnat additional quantity of rain last year were easily understood, as well aa the beneficial effects of the decrease during last month. Ile feared that 1879 was aln Ot (lisantrous year to I those engaged in agriculture. bath owners and occupiere. There are some who believed the English farmer cannot successfully compete in food production with bis rival in the Western World, hut he had no misgivings on that score, provided we were blessed with average seasons. He admitted that it was impossible to farm at a profit with such seasons as last year, but the one just passed gave sure hopes of better &

div.head: EXAMINER
div.p: THE EXAMINER
SAITHDAY SEPTEMBER 25, 1880.

Rowl.d Hill, the postal reformer, was • bene- factor, if ever there was one. He gave to his country a scheme that revolutionised the whole syetem of postal communication, and he had to struggle against stupidity and bigotry to eecnre lie adoption. But he won. He lived to me his scheme ramify from chore to shore, carrying in its train a development of trade sod commerce inch as the world had novae before witnessed. When with its firm grip death 'seised bite, the Pres, teemed with aoknowledgments that Rowland Hill had not lived in •ain, but had left the world better than he had found it. Au effort was made to raise by public subscriptions • fund for pro- miring a permanent national memorial of him but the reeponee to app.le was weak. Some small con- tributions did flow from the pockets of the publio to the promoters of the proposed memorial, end to augment them the employed in the various poet offices lathe kingdom had recourse to the holding of concerts. We eatinot help feeling that had Rowlosti Hill not devoted his energies to • work that Lao enburged the business interimnts of the .untry, conferred an incalcalable boon upon his countrymen by giving them a ch.p made et communication, and provided an invaluable channel for the spread of knowledge, but had spent his days amid the din and smoke of battle, cutting arid carving his fellow creatures into min.meat at the eapricioua dictates of ambitious and filibustering statesmen, and despoiling the habitations of dusky race, that he might win the fleeting approbation of the world for what it clans heroism, subeeriptions to the fund for perpetuating his memory would have been both more numerous and munificent, whilst the country's exchequer would probably have been drained to recognise his worth by making pensions to generation after generation of his offspring. Such is the way of the world. Sir Rowland Hill, however, has left be- hind him, in the enecessful working of his great scheme, a more prominent and lasting national monu- ment than any marble statute that may gram the in- tern or of Watt:Muster Abbey, or relieve the monoto- nous aspect of a London equare. By dint of perseverance, however, the promoters of the memorial hind have succeeded in collecting from the whole country the,sitm of £16,000. Of this emu it is pro- posed to spend £2,000 in the erection of • marble eatoe either in the rear of the Royal Exchange or within the time-honoured walls of the Abbey at Westminster. The remainder of the fund is to be applied to the csarying out of a plea for establishing almshouses for old servants of the poet-office, pros riding a sub-committee which has been appointed cm induce the Premier to reconsider the decision of ' the Treasury declining to apply an old disused poet office fund, amounting to about £30,000, to that per. pme. Should Hr. Gladstone refuse to set aside that , decision the proposal to found aleashouace will be abandoned.

Another South African war is brewing, and it is the outcome, just as the Zulu outrage woe the result, of needle.. intermeddling by Sir Bartle Freer with niece with which we were on terrne of amity. Ever innee the inhabitanta of Baautoland acknowledged the sovereignty of Eng land's Queen in 1868, the Basuto& have proved themselves loyal subjeote ; and they have been permitted until now to carry arm to protect theta- whom and their flecks, or or personal badge. of bawl... The Bellaoe never showed any driporition I to make any use of those arms to free themeelvee from British domination until Sir Bartle Freer in- &iced the Cape Government to join him in the aite.mpt to set warlike tribes within and without the pale of British rule by the tare that he :night gratify an &bawd ambition to shine aa a mighty potentate before barbarians, and make them be- lieve that he held their destiny in bin hands. The colonial authorities were worked into a condition of diatruet by a report that Cetewayo wee anxious to "wash the epeara " of hi, bearer; and the world knows that thousands of bodies of British aoldiers now lie in the roil of Zululand victims of a useless red unneceseary war provoked under the excuae of that pretended distrust. The real ground for coarting hostilities was to tionomplinh an idle scheme for confederating the South African Staten The Transvaal, the country of the Boers, was wised for Una end, and war was carried Into I Cetewayo's dominion for a like purpose. to keep. leg with this policy of annexation, and the desire to break the power of neighbouring tribes. the Cape Government, in trying to solve the awkward problem Sir Bartle Faure kart.' and Jett behind hire mfinialood, ordered tbe Beatrice to lay down their arras. The Beaconsfield ,Government warned the Cape Miniatry of the folly of thin rrouedure, end intimated in plain term that if they found there. melee, plunged into the trouble they were an- doubtedly inviting by their aation, they must nog kelt to Feigleud to get them out of their difficulties.

hut must fight their own may through the perplexities they would raise. When the Gladstone Govetathetat oatse into officio, Load Kimberley, the Colonial Seevetary, clearly pointed I oat to the Cepa Miniatry that it the order for di. armament wao attempted to be enforced against the I Boautos, and the latter reeiated, no English troops I would be sent to aid them in misquoting the N.A., ' but they would be left to bear the brunt of provoking the native. of 13aantoland into acts of hoetility. The Cape Government, however, stupidly persists in ' currying out its euteidal programme, and probably Ito persistence is due to a suspicion that, despite Warning, and avowals, England will never nutter humiliation to betel her colonial forcee ; but it is likely that the colonists will have an awakening in which they mill realise that their enspicions have been groundless. The Cape Government her already ventured to achieve it. object, and despite the willingness of the Basutoa to come to an amicable arrangement it recently sent a detachment, con- siating of seventy men, of the Cape Monnted Eiflea, under the command of Captain Carrington, to invade the land of the Smut.. Twelve thousand native* assembled to rmeive them, and the invaders lost three Of their number, including Lieutenant Clark. It ia dated that the losee, of the BuntOe were consider- able. When the invading force was attacked it was engaged in reconnoitering a village of a native chief named Serothodi, whom Sir Bartle Preto had pre- vlonsly threatened to street. It may now be taken that we are launched into another of those numerous little ware" that we have so often been engaged in in South Africa; and what the upshot will be it is impassible to foretell, seeing that the draggle has been entered into by the Cape Ministry with the Iknowledge that they mart not look for sap port from : England, and that while the colonists can only send into the field an army of at moot three thousand the : Bando, can meet them with thirty thousand fighting

WlO.l has got quit, at least for two months, of a Ravage that would put an uncivilised Zulu to the blush. Thin Englints barbarian in a promising young man, named John Fairclough, and his domentia felicity he has enjoyed in the neighbourhood of Silver-street. Entering the Silverwell Hotel he called fora glans of beer and then acquainted the landlord, Joseph Ash- emit, that he would "pouch" him, and " du" five yeara for the job. He leaped the counter and made a ferocious attack upon Ashcroft, whose head and arms he " punched " with his feet in conformity with the Wigan faehion. Under the impresaion that "punch- ing" was not sufficient maltreatment for a publican, he endeavoured to break one of Aifficroft's tburiabs. Ashcroft tried to compel his assailant to let go his hold by biting onel of, Fairclougles .fingem, and from that moment a disgueting biting contest ensued. Fairclough seined the publican's nom with bin teeth, and subsequently jammed ths head of the object of bin spleen "op nod down" on the flour until somebody wan induced to take • merciful view of the situation of the victualler, scia to put • atop to the disguating brutality. The matter waa brought before the notice of the looal justices, and for two months Fairclough will now have over the execution of hard labour Maks, opportunities for reflecting what a sorry specimen he is of nineteenth century eivilination.

flint question in the minds of many people in Widnes, whether the School Board of that town have pursued a wine course in taking upon themselves to sagged to the Local Beard that they ought to immediately abolish, at least wash, their hands of any connection with the fair. Several reasons hog been alleged by member, of the School Board why this coarse should be pursued, the principal of which seems to be that it seriously affects the attendance of children at school, the secondary one being that it. tendency is in. moral. The first reason hoe not been established in any satisfactory mwner, for upon this point the members of the educational body could not even agree among themselves Mn. Deacon arguing that it could not be proved by the figures available as a basis for consideration of the matter, that the fair materially affected the attendance of children. When a doctors "differ, who is to decide? Surely not the Local Beard. Liens suppose, for an instant, that the fair does somewhat affeet the attendance of children at school ; even then it only lags for about three days, and it is not likely that the non-attendance of • few of the !scholars at that particelar time is likely to seriously damage the prospects of the schools when those in atten- dance come to be men by the Government Inspector. Speaking snore who Ise had coneiderable to do with educe. tional matters, I should be inclined to assert, somewhat emphatically, that the long holidays given to the wholes have far more to do with the difficulty experienced in get- ting many no them into the higher standards, for any else who knows anything of teaching la ewers that *ft.- the in- tellects of the children have been in a fallow state torn many weeks, it necesaarilv takes about a fortnight to get them up to the point at wl;leh they good before the holi- days. It would bra wise thing if the holidays in the case eatl children attending school could be shortened somewhat. Then we have the argument about the immorality. Pro- bably there la scarcely any amusement not attended by some etight immorality, owing to the natural tendency of human nature to go to extreme.. Major Cr,.., the chairman of We Local Board, is reported to have need the !Ailing words during the dimuesime at the meeting over whi presided. —s He we, of opinion that the attention of the hoot Board should be called to what he considered was the etrongeet argument in favour of holding the tale on the ground op- ; punier their offices, viz., that, if it were not held, there was nothing whatever to prevent the people who frequented it I vieitingWidnee, and holding their gathering on any vacant spec° of land. This the people would no doubt he able to get, as they did at St. Helene, at which town they hired ground when they were not under any regulations. Coder the plan pursued by the Local Board, all who 'gaited the fair were under their regulations, aud it wee an open ques- tion whether such a method sem not 4 hatter one than the one adopted at St. Helene." This irk net for the School Board to crack, which, I understand, they did not try [ode.' with at their meeting on Thormlay. The rematke of Major Cross are full of strong common sense. If there is to be • fair, era gathering of the people who make • living at meh • time, let it be under the control of the Local Boned, whom officials can prevent anything unmendy being allowed standing room. Ido not dispute that there are some things to be wen at each at time to which exception might be taken, but whenever wee there a scene of joyklity where there woe not something which some Mr. Solemn-Sidee might condemn. I have hmed men argue that many young ladies went to church or chapel for no other purpose than to nest their Romeo. ; that class meetings—most solemn gatherings if properly conducted..- ! were only similar places of meeting ; and ae for flood Templar lodges, that they were complete sinks of iniquity. There am weaknesses about GI human organisation, even ' when they are intended tore good end, and the man who Its ' inclined to pick out the follies connected with them has , not a very difficult Leek. Not that I would place such things as going to church or chapel one par with attending • pleamre fair, and I hope tltte inference will not be drawn I by any captious readex What lam coming to in my argu- . ment is this, that if eeerything by which money is made was to be severely sifted este It, tendency, then many good ; and tree men if they decided to have nothing to do with anything but what had a pure ten- dency, would have to stop doing • great proportion of their trade; and, therefore, that though the fair mar be quite open to the criticisms made upon it, yet if it is to be held, why should net the Local Board pocket the profits rather than some primer landowner. Take the ease of • stationer whose duty it is to provide hie customers with what they Irak. They order each papers! as Sperling Life, ! the works of writer. whom productions the seller may be , looks upon with abhorrence: some of them want "The Sacred Heart," being Boman Catholics, and he believes the Holy Fearer is the leader of people who believe a lie; the Unitarian aske for the works of Harriet Martineau, and the ! Secularist for those ef Bradlaugh, and I will suppose that , my bookseller inn good Churchman, and • firm believer in the damnatory classes of the Athenasiw Creed. What in to be done? Is the bookseller justified in selling what his cus- tomer want.? I think he is, though some moralige would say he was not. Take another ow. A Seemed victualler who is himself a respectable citizen anddom not want to add tothe mieery of the country., mile that which, according to a horough-feced obtainer, is the GUM of nearly all the misery afflicting the country. tithe publican called upon to eit down , and think what evil Uses themirits he mlle,which may begood if properly used, may he put to ; or is the gunsmith to cease selling revolrers because one purchaser out of 50 may blow his brains out with one At the last meeting ef the Local • Board, Mr. Barrow took up the ground that If the fair were to he attacked, the encouragement et !similar visitors to those who came to it at such a gathering as the Farnworth Agricultural Society, which was patronised by the Vicar of Farnworth and nth, clergy and ministers of all denomina-1 lions," oaght to be put a stop to. At the meeting of the I School Board on Thuredity I ender/nand that a rather long I discussion took place on the letter alleged to have been sent by Mr. Corey to that body asking for statiatics showing how the fair affected the attendanceof children at school. During the debate for. O'llmffe, who is on the Loral Board, mid he might say that s the members of that Board coneidered it • piece of Impertinence en the part of the School Board to interfere in matters which concerned the Local Board."' The good intentions of the School Board cannot be ques- tioned, but the wisdom of the course they have pursued in Irving to teach the Local Board, compared with which they thenselvm may be said to be but sef yesterday," their busi- ness, may with fah-nese be questioned. I any this without at the same time committing myself to any opinion upon the merits or demerit. of what 1 known as .tthe fair."

Many of the ratepayers of Widnes will no doubt be a little surprised to hear that Mr. Martin Taylor stated, at the meeting of the School Board on Thursday, that he did not intend to offer hitneclf n a candidate at the election whgh will take place in the course of a few weeks. At the mere time that gentleman brought an important matter before the meeting vie., the great difficulties under which the Ileat election was conducted. He alleged, and ap- pears to hare been strongly supported In his allege- titau, that ratepayas desiring to rsoord their votes

Tise first Noncon- formist burial in the Ctinrch of England portion of the Cemetery took place on Friday afternoon, when the remains of the late Mrs. Burrows, of Tanners Lane, were interred In Ike family grave. - --- A FREE LIBRARY FOR ErNCORN. Sr,—Al the annual meeting of the Runcorn Literary' and Mechanics' Institute, held lost week, the rritestion of the library was brought forward. It was figaLgr, after aorne talk, that the members of the Inalitute,llslllllll of bding the mere custodian. c.f the public library, were the proprietors of it. A trust deed wee to have been drawn up many years ego, by which the library was to be held in toilet by then. for the public benefit, but by mine remiseneee it was over- looked and therefore the ',bole of the books are practically in the posaemion of the Institute. It was shown at the meet- ing referred to that the library wan not put no that use which it might be, and that it wae originally intended it ehould be and there wee. unanimous feeling In favour of turning the library over to the town, if • scheme cruild be minted out by which such an institution as a free I rbrary might be instituted on a sound barns. Relieving that Shakspere's remark about taking the tide at the flood appliee to com- munities as well as individsala, I beg to mil attention to Lryflurable opportunity which now prevent. itself for I making • fair Kart in the direction of the formation Of • public reading room and free library for tlie town of Runcorn. It is utterly imposrihte for ir or --e to r.riflette the advautagm which a pulrlic ',Mary .f , . It ' would offer the mean, of enriching the mind by study and recreation; and by elcratinr the eloodard of education it would give the bromine of in't.gari,r,, arin, and thereby amply repay tbe tax-payer for any outlay in tbe ahape of rates. Vice and crime are fearfully expensive weed, to allow to grow ; and Re prevention it 'better than cure, steps • shoeld be taken to counteract such noxion. growths. The , remedy in an immense degree lies close to hand, if ere ham, but the courage and public spirit to apply it. The paean of the Free Libraries' Act" fhrnishel the machinery, by I means of which no institution can, with little trouble totti lees experme, be formed which shall am ea • centre of light and influence, the good effecte a which will tell on the present and HI future generations. On the 25th of lag month • free library was opened in trldham--the gift of • local manufacturer and not long ago the Earl of Derby opened a simil.ienitution in Blackpool. I wneld recom- mend anyone who is wavering as to the ridvimbility of form- ing a library in Runcorn to pay a visit to the Norton read- ing room, Liverpool. I ant sure the visit will whet him literary appetite and lead 4iirn to the determination to do his very utemet towards getting n like boun for Runcorn. I should like ti call attention to your report of r befit. Helene Town Council which appeared in Inn week En:twitter, With special reference to thc librarian'e anneal report. 'The estimated expenditure foe the coming year is a little over f.,400, which includes f.. 200 for the purchase of new booka. Such an amount for a town of the sax of kr, Helene is • mere bagatelle r arid there Hirruld be no heeitarion whatever on the part of the leading gentlemen of Hareem, in setting about nurtnorialining the Chairman of the Commissioner., and taking the opinion of the ratepayers on the questions. I It is idle to talk as °Flacons" did a few weeks ago, about I individual philanthropy in the matter—" who would be I free, himself miter rtrike the blow." It in for Om good of the public at large, and each individual ought ha feel his share of the responsibility which attache. to his position AB one of the cornmunity. Hoping that this queetion will receive the attention it deserves, I remain, yours, A 13001( WORM.

. _ SAVAGE ASSAULTS AT WARRINGTON.' At the Warrington Borough Polies Court on Tuesday morning last, before Alderman Webster and Councillor Broadbent, Jame. Foster, an engine tenter, living at 57, Greenell-st., was charged under arrest with having unlaw- fully wounded hie wife, Sarah Foster, the previous day, by cutting her with a knife, and with intent Cody her grievous bodily herrn. It appeared from the statement of Mr. Hunt, the chief crwstable, that the prisoner, who is employed at ye... Roberts, Dale, and Co.'. works, was working on the "night shift " the previous evening. About nine o'clock the prosecuaix sent his supper, afterwards going out to the shop of a Mrs. Newton. Returning home about ball-past eleven she noticed her hueband sranding near the hover", and accosted him by .tying, " Hullo, Jim." at which Si. pri- soner, whined saying a word, sprung at her with a knife,l and indicted Several severe wounds on the face. She was! farther kicked by the prisoner, and rendered insensible. She was afterwards taken to the Intinnery, and her wounds attended h, by the house surgeon. Oath. prisoner being , :wrested and charged with the offence he said, "lie a Ire', you have just used the knife as moth as Inv." He had 3 knife upon biro when arrested. Sarah Foster, the wife of the prisoner, corroborated the stateme,n, of the chief constable, end identified a pocket- knife preduced as the instrument that bed causol the wounds. Ann Newton, a widow, keeping a coal etaith in Orchard- street, Meted that about ten o'clock the previous evening the proaecutrin came to her house and stayed until about eleven I o'clock. About ten minutes alter she .me beck, bleeding, and without either bonnet or shawl. Sire was covered with blood, and stated that her husband had done it with a knife. She appear,' the worse for beer, but witness could not asp she was drunk. Charles bonnet Richmond, surgeon at the Warrington Infirmary, deposed that on that morning, about one o'clock, the po.srcutrix was brought to the Infirmary. Ile found an alsed wound about an inch long unite through the left tril and another on Si. outaide of the nose. She had also lack eye and a brnise on the left anti, prisuner,,in answer to the usual charge, said, "I came home last even* because my little girl had come to the works crying, and wying she could not net in. I went horne and found my wife coming home almost drunk. I never used the knife." He was then committed to take Iris trial at the next Liver- pool asnizes, bail being accepted for his appearance.

James Commley, a farm labourer, was charged under a remand with unlawfully woundingone Elizabeth Townley on the 15th September. The prisoner pleaded not guilty. The Chief Constable mated that the protecutria was the wife of John Townley, a labourer, who reaides at 55, Coon- dry-M., and the prisoner IA a fano labourer at Bortonwood and living in Bay Horse Yard, off Winarick-et. The back ' door of the prosecutriz'a house goes into Bay Horse Yard, and a water closet is also in that yard, totter to which it i 3 necessary 0 pear the place where the prisoner lodges. On the day in question the prosecutria sear passing through Bay Horse Yard, when the defendant, who was atandiog at his ovro door, accosted her by mying, "You old b---, you would not come for a witness yesterday, but we have done without you." The prisoner, who had a rolling pie in his hard, then struck the woman aorosa the nose, felling her to she ground and rendering her eenseless. The prosecutri)CS husband was entering the yard at that moment and saw the blow struck. Information was at once given to the point, sod the prisoner was arrest, d. The woman was taken to the istitrinary, where her wounds were attended to. The proaecutria deposed to the statement given above ; tad Dr. Richmond, of the Infirmary, stated that the woman was brought in to the Infirmary on the night of the 13th amt. Her nose was completely smashed in, and she was bleeding very much. • The prisoner, in answer to the charge, still he was sitting io the house on the nightie question and heard the prose- oaths calling Lint had names in a house across the yard. He went ht the door and wanted to know why site was tog him, when she came up to hint and seized him by the 'shirker.. Ile then strock her across the nose with his fist, .tod she fell to the ground. He was committed to gaol .for one month with bard 'Amer.

It appeared that Elizabeth Williams, wife of Samuel Williams, was standing at her door between twelve and one o'clock on Sunday morning het. when she heard a smash of glass. She olwerved a moldier immediately after, coming from Mr. Burgess's with three bottles in his hands. He was walking leisurely along carrying the bottles. A Nom. Dams.—A novel and exciting race tank place the other evening not a hundred miles from Premot. Fired with emulation, two well-known individuals not lack- ing in vigour if unendued with full limb power, matched themselves to contract in the dark. The excitement was grmt ; odds ran up in consequence of the novelty of the race and the quality of the racers. An enthusiastic, ever- uniting starter was instantly appointed; a lantern was speedily obtained, and with each face wreathed in smiles, seen from the light of that lantern, the ron,sye proceeded to a pleasant avenue. The anxiety prevailing can beet be deecribed in the words of a bystander, '• By gow, awm blest if this too due no beat th' Darby!" What a picture that couple of athletes preeented as they gradually melted in the darkness, preceded be the stalwart nterter, still smiling, with the lantern bobbing at his shins The excitement increased, though one was beard to remark, le Eh, chaps, lei met Le waiting fort be hung ;" Dowd thi nise,” said another, " bean con we hear irn coml." At last steps were heard approaching. "Ston heck, everybody, we cone. see him," IV.Ir the rev, and in • moment appeared the well-known form ' of the winner. Ile was shouldered, the scene cloeed, so did the lantern, and silence reigned.

The Ctrtm gated that with reference to the deficiencies at the workhoues, he had sent to the Local Government Board, the following letter which he bed drawn up in ac- cordance with instructions received from tbe Board. "To the Local Government Board, Whitehall, London, 31 August.— My Lords and Gentleineo,—l am directed by the Guardians of this Union to acknowledge the receipt of your letter of the 24th inst., respecting their request for an inspector to Institute an enquiry into the general management of the workhouse. I am to inf ern you that at a meeting of the Greardians held on Thursday last, • committee was appointed for the purpose of preparing, and laying before you a specific statement as to the management. The committee met yesterday when I was diricted to eubmit to you the following - —l. That the Master mid the Matron have departed from the prescribed dietary, in giving bacon instead of beef. 2. That the Matron informed the Guardians that she had knowingly given out bacon is place of beef witheut the Master's orders or instructions, and that she had !given out these articles for the last ten weeks, with two es three exceptions. 3. That on the stock being taken on the :Ist and 23r1 of June lag, it was , found in a very unsatisfactory gate ; the spirits had been diluted, and the Matron acknowledged that she bad had en- tire charge of them, and Haat she had burnt the " permits." There wm a deficiency in the flannel account of 200 yards. 4. That the Master's weekly provision account hook shown that 8,360 pounds of beef and mutton have been received during the last 10 weeks, whereas 11,7E3 pounds appear to have been given out during that period. 5. That the Matron has only once during two years and five months visited the wards in the hospitals under No. Leathern's charge, and only once in twelve months in the ward of Nurse Clarke 6. That clothing has frequently been applied for and not obtained for Nurse Leathern* Clarke'., and Horn- Iby'a ward., end the patients have been compelled to lay in bed In consequence. 7. That an inmate named Ann Tales , was lamed in January last by the Matron. The committee consider the foregoing sufficient to cause yrni to institute an enqutry.—Youre, 40., S. IL HAHTLIIT, Clerk." ST. HELENS.

' A most interesting and enjoyable lecture with the above tide was delivered by the Her. W. 0. Simpson, of Ilkley, Yorkehire, under the auspime of the Nutgrove Wesleyan Chapel, in the Town 11.11, St. Helene, on Tuesday evening last. The lecture was in every sense a treat and was listened to with close attention. There wit. a fair audience. Admission wee by ticket, the proneeds going towards a new chapel for the Nutgrove Weeleyans. Dr. McNicol oceupied the chair, and there were also on the platform, the Rees. J. A. B. Harry, W.ll. Paacoe, W. C. Tayler, and T. Wilshaw ; Mr. Councillor Walker, Messrs. T. Hewitt, J. Lyon, J. T Anderton, he. There were also present in the body of the ball, Messrs. J. Cook, T. Cook, T. Robinson, anti Walker (of Earleetown.) The CHAIRMAN said he had • pleasure in introducing to threes lecturer who could gratify them, one who could fill their hearts and their heads too, and satisfy the whole of the cravings of the audience, and would aesureally increase their fervency and enthusiasm. To make a euccessful meeting two or three element,' were requisi.—• good lecture end a good subject. The lecturer was assured to them, because they had tasted his quality before, but he did not know much abont Sammy Hick, except that be knew he was a great character. Must of them were but ordinary common place people, but " Sammy " was an exceptienal character, and those two elements coupled with a good cause, that of raising funds for Nutgrove chapel, would ensure a emcees, of the meeting. Nutgrove chapel was an old ship that had made many good voyages, and taken many from this shin of the waters and landed them safely on the opposite shore. I. memories were sacred and its walls also, but there came times when eld things wore out and new ones were wantel and young men who took an interest in the place were desire,oe of havine a sew place. They were doing • great work for the town, and he hoped they wonld attain the ultimatum of their hopes. (Apple...) The LFCI,IIIIR, after making some preliminary observe- Nene, said the village blacksmith was a great and good lean. It wan I.cause he fell in with the line at Divine purpose and Providence in the ...gement and government of His church. God had n chosen the :Fmk things of this worl,l to confound the mighty; and the things that are despised and the things th it are not to move the Ulises that are," which meant that God hod chosen things, as they would soy, that were good for nothing, to bring to nothing things that they thought were something. Sammy Hick WAS born in a village about 13 miles from Leer., and was one of 13 chil- dren,. that it was a matter of doubt whether his father Has glad to can him. (Laughter.) It woe not always the case torn father to be glad under nuch circumstances. He did not know that he over went to school, hut he rather thought there was no intellectual activity at all at work in the blacksmith before he received the spark of divine glace When writing he always used plenty of paper, and he (the lecturer) had a great number of his letters, hut there was nothing smaller than a fool:peep sheet amongst them. (Laughter.) It appeared alne that he had mistaken a hedge stake for spec, and he might have used the words of the Apostle Paul to the Galatians "Ste hew in large letters I have written unto you." (Renewed laughter ) At fourteen years of age he was apprenticed to a blacksmith!and cartel with many good quelities to ensure his success in life. He was industrious, he was kindly in his manner, and in the third place he was good looking, and this was net an un- important particular between the age of 14 and N). He was never lodgeml to his father for a single penny during the whole time of hie apprentice- ship. Sammy mid that everybody woe kind to him, and he (the lecterer) was not surprised at it. There was an old proverb which said "ho that would hare friends should show himself friendly," and Sammy was kind to 1 everybody. The ledturer hat met with many men who I would say .ah, they are a proud, exclusive lot ; I won't go ' there any more ;" and he had add to such men, "How did you manage when you went there the tiret time? did you walk down the aisle, Mewling six foot, saying to yourself e I sheuld not like anybody to speak to tne; I will let them know I am as goml ea they are ; or did they go with • sunny look?" Ile generally found those words to be true—"be kind to no ono, and noon. will be kind toyou." (Hear, hear.) As to hisgool looks, he might so, he had never wen him ; put he bed the very beat evidence, for his master's daughter fell in love with him. (Laughter.) He hoped that was conclusive. Mr. Darby one night came down stairs 'and fourd Sammy sitting—some authorities said upon a chair, some of them said upon the handle, but it really did not matter, for there wan no doubt as to where she was sitting ehe was sitting upon Saninly'e knee. (Great laughter and cheers.) liens, very wrry to hmr that clap. It node him welder what kind of Young gentleman and ladies they were. However, Mr. Darl,y, haying seen what he did see, he hastily retrmted to his bedroom and acquainted his wife with the circuits- stancee, adding in pure Yorkshire "1 ay believe mwr lass is as fond o' yon lad as ever aeon won of a coal." (Loud laughter.) He mei not say that the indentures were can- celled the following day, and poor Sammy left the smithy behind him and went out into the world. For 12 months he was a gentleman ebout town. When 21 years of age his father procured a little elnithy for l,itw nmr Micklesfield, and lie was sorry to any that little smithy had been pulled I down, for twelve months ago the stone masons were at work, , and it waa now hnproved " off the face of the earth." The ! lecturer went on Co say that having paid for his ! tools he was left without a penny in the world, but with industry combined with honesty. he prospered and procured a piece of domestic furniture,' .metimes called a helpmeet. (Laughter.) He was • , . musical blackemith, and sat M the choir of the parish church. There were very curious things going on in sing- ' ing pews. (Laughter.) One Sunday he saw somebody ) who he thought would do, and he slipped into the church- , yard and waited until Martha came by, when he dropped in • by her side, and—nobody tells of anybody else, bemuse if • anylady is worth his colt be W 0111—" whiepered to her his sweet ictentlone." After that they delighted in each other's t company; of course they did. (Laughter ) Martha was then only 313; they went to the hymeneal altar aud were t married. They did not get on very well at first, bemuse , Martha was seven ymrs his senior when they married, and • was 'even years alder over after. (Laughter.) She became dictateriel, and was regular in her habits. Sannev, being simple-hearted, was always doing such grand and eccentric things. The reeult was they fell out, for, to us: a very polite • expremion, them was incompatibility of temper. (Laugh- ; ter.) lielutiful words! But they dip not talk like that at • Micklmfleld; the neighbours said, f h.rd Sammy and • 31atty hey bin hatching." Soon, morning Sammy stalked off with the intention of never coming hack ; but he did turn back, for, said he, When I saw the bonny green fields and the white lambs, I couldn't mak up mi mind to leave them." ) His tenderneas of heart wae there shown. Things went on until he wee 29 years of age, and people never had a thought , that he would have a history. It was a mieerable thing to ! • reflect how inany p.ple there were who died without a I • history. If he were only to sit himself down he could write ) the history of most, p.ple on oae side of. sheet of paper. , He then described Sammy's conversion, after hearing 31r. I Wesley preach. After being in bed with hie wife for Rome time, he rolled out of bed, and began groaning for mercy. His poor wife, Martha, thought there was something the matter with hint, and began to look for the flint, tinder, and match., which were very seldom found together ; and while elle went chip, chip, chip, Sammy was on the . hearthstone with his voice penetrating the sky. The 1 lecturer', had been to two out of three of the great Handel! , festival, and it had been a melancholy thing to reflect how 1 far the music row. Ile was afraid it did not go very much ! higher than the topmmt :mire of the tower, lot when Sammy , sat there his ballet:lie!,e went into the very windows of the heavens, and angels rejoiced tied a sinner had repented. (Applause.) Although six feet one in his Mocking feet he did not Appear so high as he really was, for long habit of , trade bent his sheulders—one a little up, and the other a little down; his countenance was fair, but the only Fidel& cant feature about 11i02 was his grey blue eyes. His lan- guage was peculiar to hi, native land, and I.indley Murray would assuredly have been puzzled with some of his words. For awaken he would any "wakken," " chllder "foe chil- , then. n I weant " for I will not, emissioners " for mis- sionaries, and " menelisees" for Methodists (Great laughter.) All these of course are very musical to every- , one who could understand them. In quite of all uncouthnees of manner and outrage...B of attire, the peculiar pro. vincAll.lllB, if a man waa a 11100 he would make lee way, I but ifs man wan perfect in his attire, faultleee in his ges- ture, with the fined acemt, and be nothing bats puppet and a doll, people would not care for him. (Applause.) It was 1 Ott long before the London chapels were open to him, and I he preached in seveml of them. attracting large congrega- tions. At the cloee of one of his sem., one of thew little , fellows called cockneys advance! towards him and said, , Ah, 1 feel very much blemed, but you know the language, you know." (Laughter.) Sammy made nothtug more to ! do but took held ef the cockney', haled as if it had been the Mickletield pump—(laughter)—gave Ito hearty shake, say- ing at the same lime, " Never heed th• language if tha nobbut get blessed." (Laughter.) At the ',resent time one would say, . Ile's an exquisite preacher the langdage is , so choice, and his articulation so perfect . I admire it ;" but to the queetion, " Do you ever get Wowed ?" the reply would be" I really—haw—L—haw—don't understand you: that in a religioue expression, I suppose." (Loud laughter.) The Lecturer went on to say that Sanamy never were brace' but once. He was introduced ton party in a dining-room, but caused a titter to run through the whole circle by con- stantly " hitching" um his unmentionable, He was taken aside ire: the good lady of the house and given a pair of braces with all the colours of the rainbow. On appearing again before the company the laughter was only greater when they beheld poor Sammy with the braces ever his waistcoat. (Laughter.) On I;ie mistalre being explained to him, Sammy resolved to dispense with braces, as he could not underetanrl the beautiful things being placed out of sight. Speaking of his courige, Mr. Simpwn related how boldly he underwent the process of bleeding after being thrown out of a cart and rendered insensible, and how Sammy deecribed the operation as being "as nice as owe" After all was over Sammy said to the doctor," The Lord hes made thee 0 great bleming to my b,edv; maybe He'll crab ! one a great bleming to thy soul ;" and they kuelt down to- gether, and if he (the lecturer) was an artist he would paint it. !Hear, hear.) The remit was the doctor deeired Samm to begin service in hie (the doctor's) kitchen; and after'. while the doctor built a chapel In the village, and it was not long ago that he (Mr. Simpson) gave this rery lecture in that very chapel with the doctor relative pitting by his girls. That woe courage; but he knew men in fo-ge and factory who could throw up their huge muscle and could fell anon with a blow. not able to my "No . to the man that wanted them te go and do ennething wrong. (Applause , Several instances of Sammy' Hick's extrmne kindnese were next given, One morning, he gave all the bre.) and , milk in the house to same aoldirrr who were on their woe to the field of Waterloo, and before Martha had come down- stairs. Many of the soldiers on the field of battle wished that the village blacksmith was neer Obese; and in the first chapel they entered on coming Mel, who ehould be the preacher but the village bleckernith, Sammy Hick ! sAp. pleuse.) His good nature often got him into Nibble with his wife, who, howeves, generally finished up Iwith Thou's a queer -Sammy, hut the best old Sammy that ever was born." In eoncluding his lectore, Mr. Simpson said I hare finished I cannot pereuerle myself it is a lecture. but think that I have had ,' the old man by the button, having a little chat. Good-hye, 1 Sammy, eood-bye. Queer old Sammy, but flae beet old Sammy that ever was born ; good.bye, Samtny, good-bye. (Cheers.) The Caisuswas said he foretold the lectaree would Ali*

A meeting of the miners of St. Helens on. held on Thom- day night, et the,Coffee Haim Tavern, to consider the Ingle question and desirability of amore pezfect organisation. ' There were • large cumber present.snd Mr Pickard not being , preaent, Mr. John Crom was appointed to the chair. The Chairman briefly opened the meeting, remarking that the , object of the meeting was to conabler combination. fie Men called upon Mt. Wood, of Ashton, who slimmed hie pleasure at teeing a chairman for reborn he once used to work as a cool shover. If they reviewed the history of the Miners Amociation, they would at once find that Lancashire bad "made lees progress than any of the other counties in , England with respect to organisation to-day. That spoke very sadly for them and showed that there was eomething 1 the matter with them in Lancashire, of which their friend. in other parts of the country were not acquainted. It , showed that there was some itdernal defect in the organise- , tion that bad been created and bad died away. Haley went • into the north of England,into Cumberland, tbaham,and into Scotland they found they were most strongt• cemented to- 'tether. The result was that when a dispute 'took place, In- stood oTthe masters ignoring the Inen• claims they met the deputation of men and omen Red with them on any particular vexed question. That was not the cam in lanmshire lie did net think they could soy that with regard to the em- ployers and employol at St. Helens, or Park lane, and if Mr. Pickard was there lie did not think he could say that with respect to Wigan. If the masters raid it must belt wonld have to be don*. The real cause was the men I ired in an I isolated rendition. There was no friendly Intercourse be- tween the men, but each worked for himself. showing the , ! want of the right spirit amongst them. The Yorkshire and , Derbyshire ruiners shortly met together in confermce and they found thit it was not sufficient for each county to be mganieed (although they were thoroughly organiied,, err Obey agreed to cement the two counties together. The I reason of the wonted organisation in this district was the jmlous feeling that eeisted amongst etch other ; they could I not put confidence in their leaders and cassequently there I hal been Bohm amongst them. Bat the union had .d.one , work mad hat been the calm of the Miner's Itagelation Act being placed on the statute book. They had bleaaings in that bill, which, had it not been for the association would never have been enjoyed by therm. The bills become, law at the ' begioing of next year. The aexoebition had also brought into existence the Employer's Liability Bill, which provided that compensation be made to. collier or servant who was , injured or killed by the incompetency or negligence of the ina.stem :or their immediate servants. It was useless for agitators to come among* the,, if they did not resort to the work of personally speaking Co the men on the .object Rod if the check-weighmen would only exert themeelves a bit, Oh,, might be most umful in organising tlie men. (A voice That is what is wanted.) In his district the check-weighman hat done well, and charged the union money along with the weigh money, and the men did not object to it, end men had been added to the eociety. The master could not touch the check-weighman so long as he did not break the Ire ; but he could do the name with other servants. lie was glad to any that in one place in St. Helens the check-man had proved of service. He :urgal upon them not to be divided but organise. Mn. Rorterr Lean- of Wigan, then addremed the meeting, and said that at the Sherdley colliery their friend Mr. Henry Cove, who waa always anxious to do what he could for them, had effected some good. .rind at the last district meeting represented 120 men and the wagoners were ap- pealing te them to loin. He would no. cane and welcome, i and before long Ise Loped erery fireman and day man would , themes well. Referring to the conference lately held he observed that they had decided tu send circulars round to their employers in different parts of the country. Mr. , Lewis. then referred to the justice which he mid was generally got in St. Helena, remarking that he had no hope for the dingoes te be satiefactorily settled until they got a stipendiary to bear their cal*, in. • stead of their employers. (Chem.) Speaking of the al- 1 vantagea they hoot from the Liability Bill, he mid that It • would prevent accidents, bemuse the masters neglected to lay out a little money in preventing the noxious gime to weed in the pit, and by working three or four seam. of coal in one pit., instead of ainking • new pit. The moult had been that there had been a great astride. of human lives. But there was reason to believe that in future this will not be the case. He advised them to get their check- weighman on their side,and mid that he would not pay a penny too weighiran who did Oct belong to the society. Mr. Cuoss next erldressed the meeting, and spoke tij.n the gases pervading the pi., olnerving that the con should have more knowledge of the danger of the different gamut Ile had been down pits when something like IS explosions had taken place, and when four to ten lives had been lost. PIANOS FOR THE MELBOURNE EXHIBITION.

The chief exhibig of British pianos at the forthcoming E Melbourne xhibi will be the celehrab titan of Mossrs. John Brinamead an Sons, who, by the way, at the recent Sydney Exhibition, gained the highest award and • special mention above sorb eminent firms as Steinways and Chickerings, of America; Erard, fiord, Codicil, and Paling, of Paris ; Bechstein, Blinbner, (inn,ntlnnr, Ascherberg, Lipp, Schiedmayer, Refinish, Neumeyer, Neufeld, and Ibllling and Spangenberg, of Germany and Pohlmann, IVotuurn, and Chappell, of England. Following up the successes they lamer gained for our country in Sydney, Messrs, John Brine- mead and Sons propose to even improve their pianos, even if being the highest) they cannot improve their posit;on, for Melbourne. A few wrek• ago they gave a public recital at St. James' Hall on the pianofortes they intend to send to Melbourne. Them pianos are not specially manufactured for the occasion. They are, indeed, takes "not of stock," although they are doubtless among the best of Meson. John Brinsmead and Son,' ordinary manufacture; such, in short, as Ate not espressly made for exhibitions, but as are sold to the general public. The first piano is what is called a' full-concert grand," anti,, in fact, the piano used for concerti, It lA in an oak case, and It has various patented improvements which we shall proceed to describe with, as far as possible, an avoidance of technicalities. The "cheek-repeater action allows tech note to be sounded as rapidly as the nimble/it pianist can play it. The " sostenctue aoundingrboard allows the whole sound-board to be used instead cf only a small portion of it, and it greatly improves the sustaining and other powers of tone. Tic" sound-sustaining pedal " allows one or more notes, ur a chord, to be sounded for a minute or more, the hammers and dampers being held from each note, while the other mites can Le enlisted indepen- dently. Other pianos to be sent to Melbourne are • grand, sultabi for drawing-rom use, with the sound-eustainins pedal before deteribed, and with bridgee of reverbration ; a ebor t iron gram! piano, a grand oblique piano, the strings of which are placed obliquely, and which, having gained a medal at Phila.. delphis, is called the ''Centennial Oblique" ; an overstrung grand oblique piano with the newly-invented tone renovator, which we shall presently describe; and au upright iron grand. All them pianos have • complete iron frame which meltes the piano last a life time, and they all lave dae e sostenente sounding.board ; and the patent "check-repeater action n already described. The special invention to be ex- hibited at Melholarne is however, the patent tone compen- sator and renovator, by which the pianoforte, which km hitherto been at a disadvantage as compared with other etringed inetrumente, mny be so modulated as to preeerve definite and equal quality of tone, which can easily be re- newed at any time, it ehould be remarked that when, for instance, the tone of a riolln deteriorates through age, or from other causes which hare nothing to do with the original soundness and perfection of the instrument the strings have lobe adjueted to a different height (inn the body of the instretnent by means of a new bridge of greater height. A similar effect is produced by the compensating mechanism in theme pianos; the strings pass over the Input the compensating bare and then on to the bridge of lite sounding board, and a series of screws regulate the position of the bars 1A may be required for the purpose of seeming or restoring complete unity and kittem of tone, the adjustinz premiere bar so controlling the pressure of the airings on the , bridges as to incsease. or diminish it at once. It would be difficult to attach too much importance to thie invention especially as it esn be applied equally well to the over-strung oblique and the upright an also to the horisontal grand pianos. An equally valuable consideration is the fact that after many years of service • piano constructed on this principle min in a few minutea be restored to ila original purity and power of tone. We mav add that Messrs. John Brinememi and Sons have, owing to the large increase in their business, I.n obliged to commence the building of an extra and large factory at Kentish Town. The new fattory will have five floors, 140 feet long by 35 feet wide, divided into fifteen workshot s. The roof will tone a magnificent flat for drying timber, this roof being ssrved by a hydraulic lift capable of lifting or lowering two tons of wood *Tromso,. Sept. Ist, 1880.

The Clerk: You are quite in error in those remarks, Mr. Taylor. The Education Department only allow one polling booth for so many, and Mr. Hartley had two election booths more than were allowed. On Thursday, two Wesleyan high eohoola or college.— the one (Hepworth College, Rbyl) for boys. and the other (Pemba, College, Colwyn Bay) for girls—were inaugurated by a mecial service held at the latter college. Payne (who presided) then introduced the Rev. Dr. Rigg, of Westminster Wesleyan College, mend. log at the head of their educational establishment." Dr. Roo° referred to a great meeting held at Abervetwith on Wednesday, and said there was a feeling for Govern- ment help on the ground of Welsh education having been neglmted. Their school, were to be supported by voluntary energies, and appealed to the consciences and to tbe intermits of thom who had to take care of and provide for their own offspring. The education which would be given would not be sectarian. while it would rest •pon the denominational organisation, character, and responsibility of the Methodist body. What they had been doing torn grett number of years without having been challenged would still he carried on--namely, providing a good Christian, Catholic education, without any aßeropt at proselytising. (Hear, bear.) He considered it a perfectly fair thing to give or receive endow- ments, en being • perfectly legitiffiate form of voluntary liberality. lint he hoped they had no need to begin to in. cline to the Government for support. (Applause.) The speaker proceeded to give the 111.1.07 of the two Institution., for which he gave mat praise to the chairman. The Rev, Dr. PrI,ISHON said the building of Pentims was dedicated about a month before. He felt the time was Come when it men necessary for them,. a branch of the unit-ems' Church not the least among the thousands of head, to assert themselves In connection with that great question of middle-clase education. They did not want their children to grow up in a spirit of intolerance and under a system where they were taught that the religion of their fathers . was founded upon an mclmiastical mistake. (Hear, hear.) . And still tree did they want thern to grow up in that latito- dinarianlinn which was akin to infidelity. div.p: CANNIBALISM AT RIXTON.
SHOCKING CASE.

At the Occasional Court House, muck-street, War- rington. yesterday, Patrick Blake no. charged before S. I Rigny, Esq., with having,on Thursday, maliciously wounded John Keating, labourer, at Rixton. The prosecutor said that on the evening of Thursday he was in the taproom of the Red Lion Inn, Riaton, and the prisoner was there also. There was a dispute about a quart of beer. A man named Joeeph Bennett came in, and the prisoner mid he would bet witness a quart of beer that Bennett had aon him. He bet primner that he had not, and asked Bennett if he had. He mid he had not. Witness said hood won his quart, but prisoner refused to pay him. He mid he would have it not of the prisoner, md struck him, but the landlady parted them. Prisoner then again attacked him, put him down on a form, struck him, and bit a piece off hie loft ear. He produced the piece, which was about an i•ch and • hall in length, and from ball to three- quarters of an inch in width. His (proeecutor's) ear bled a good deal, an I was very sore. He went to the doctor's shortly after it happened. He had not then found the piece that was bitten from his mr, bat it wasafterwards brought to him. He went and gave information at the police elation shortly otter nine o'clock. Thomas Suuon, joiner, Hollins Green, gave simiLar evi- dence, and Matel that the priemer pointed to his teeth and took the piece of the proseeutor's ear from his mouth saying he would keep it foe. month and put it in his pocket. P.C. Berry proved apprehending the prisoner who, in reply to the charge, said .1 did it in welf defence. lie struck me three time. in the face not was sitting down. I told him I couldn't fight as I had bean hurt in the side." The prisoner wits committed to take his trial at the Liver- pool quarter 8038i0111.
